examples.knowledge_point: Calculating a Limit at Positive or Negative Infinity Using L'Hopital's Rule
examples.worked_solution:
In this case, we have an indeterminate form of type $\dfrac{\infty}{\infty},$ so applying  L'Hopital's rule yields

$$
\eqalign{
\lim_{x\to \infty}  \dfrac {x^6}{5x^6-4} &= \lim_{x\to\infty}  \dfrac {[x^6]'}{[5x^6-4]'}\
&= \lim_{x\to \infty}  \dfrac {6x^5}{5(6x^5)-0}\
&=  \lim_{x\to \infty}  \dfrac {1}{5}\
&= \dfrac{1}{5}.
}
$$

feedback.worked_solution:
Here the limits of the numerator and denominator are ${lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{1}{x}=\infty $ and ${lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\operatorname{cot}⁡x=\infty ,$ respectively, so we have the case $\frac{\infty }{\infty }.$

Applying L'Hopital's rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{(\frac{1}{x})}{\operatorname{cot}⁡x} & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{{[\frac{1}{x}]}^{′}}{{[\operatorname{cot}⁡x]}^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{(-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})}{-{csc}^{2}⁡x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})}{(\frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡x})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡x}{{x}^{2}} \\  & ={({lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{x})}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

This time, the resulting limit gives the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}.$ To find the limit, we apply L'Hopital's rule once again. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{(\frac{1}{x})}{\operatorname{cot}⁡x} & ={({lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{x})}^{2} \\  & ={({lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{[\operatorname{sin}⁡x]^{′}}{[x]^{′}})}^{2} \\  & ={({lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{1})}^{2} \\  & ={(\operatorname{cos}⁡0)}^{2} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$
